questions.prompt: Which parameter declaration actually behaves as a forwarding reference capable of binding both lvalues and rvalues?
options: template <class T> void f(const T&& x);
template <class T> void f(std::vector<T>&& x);
template <class T> struct Holder { void put(T&& x); };
template <class T> void f(T&& x);
questions.explanation: Under [temp.deduct.call], T&& is a forwarding reference only when T is a cv-unqualified template parameter deduced for that exact function call. Adding const, wrapping in vector<T>, or using an enclosing class template's T produces a plain rvalue reference.

questions.prompt: Given `template <class T> void relay(T&& arg)` called with `int count = 7; relay(count);`, what are T, the declared type of arg, and the value category of expression `arg` inside relay?
options: T is int&, arg has type int&, and expression arg is an lvalue
T is int, arg has type int&&, and expression arg is an xvalue
T is int&, arg has type int&&, and expression arg is an lvalue
T is int, arg has type int&, and expression arg is a prvalue
questions.explanation: Passing an lvalue `count` deduces T = int& ([temp.deduct.call]). Reference collapsing turns T&& (int& &&) into int& ([dcl.ref]), and as a named variable `arg` is an lvalue.

questions.prompt: Why does constructing `p2` from non-const `p1` fail to compile (or select the wrong constructor) below?
options: Defaulted copy constructors cannot coexist with template constructors
Person(S&&) is explicit while copy construction requires an implicit constructor
The template constructor deduces S = Person&, which is an exact match that beats Person(const Person&)'s qualification conversion
std::forward<Person&>(p1) returns a moved-from Person
questions.explanation: Because `p1` is a non-const `Person` lvalue, `Person(S&&)` instantiates `Person(Person&)`, which requires no `const` qualification conversion and beats `Person(const Person&)` in overload resolution—then fails trying to construct `std::string` from `Person&`.

questions.prompt: What happens when calling `forward_to_vec({1, 2, 3})` where `forward_to_vec` takes `T&&`?
options: T deduces to std::initializer_list<int>, constructing std::vector<int>
Compilation fails because a braced-init-list is a non-deduced context for T&&
T deduces to int[3] and converts to std::vector<int>
Compiles only if T&& is replaced with const T&
questions.explanation: Unlike `auto x = {1, 2, 3};`, template deduction against a bare `T&&` parameter cannot deduce `std::initializer_list` from a braced-init-list ({...} is a non-deduced context under [temp.deduct.call]).

questions.prompt: Why does `std::forward<T>(arg)` use `std::remove_reference_t<T>&` in its parameter instead of deducing `T` from `arg` automatically?
options: Inside the forwarding function, `arg` is always an lvalue; deducing T from `arg` would always yield an lvalue reference and lose whether the caller passed an rvalue
Template parameters can never be deduced for functions inside namespace std
std::remove_reference_t<T>& prevents std::forward from accepting const objects
Automatic deduction would trigger copy elision on `arg`
questions.explanation: By placing `T` inside the non-deduced type `std::remove_reference_t<T>&`, `[forward]` forces callers to pass the outer deduced `T` explicitly—preserving the distinction between `T = U&` (caller gave lvalue) and `T = U` (caller gave rvalue).

questions.prompt: What does the C++ standard specify for `std::forward<int&>(42)`?
options: Returns a dangling int& bound to temporary 42
Implicitly converts 42 into a static storage int so the reference stays valid
Ill-formed: the rvalue overload of std::forward mandates `!std::is_lvalue_reference_v<T>`
Returns an int prvalue by decaying the reference
questions.explanation: Under [forward], the overload `template<class T> constexpr T&& forward(remove_reference_t<T>&& t)` mandates that `is_lvalue_reference_v<T>` is `false`. Passing an rvalue (`42`) while requesting an lvalue-reference `T` (`int&`) is explicitly ill-formed.
